# Voiceverse NFT plagiarism scandal

The **Voiceverse NFT plagiarism scandal** was a 2022 controversy in which the blockchain-based voice synthesis start-up Voiceverse was reported to have used audio generated by the non-commercial text-to-speech project 15.ai without permission or attribution, and to have marketed and sold the resulting clips as original non-fungible token (NFT) voice assets. The incident came to public attention in January 2022, shortly after prominent video game voice actor Troy Baker announced a partnership with Voiceverse to promote “voice NFTs”, and it intensified broader criticism of NFT projects and commercial applications of generative artificial intelligence (AI).

The creator of 15.ai, a pseudonymous artificial intelligence researcher known as 15, identified Voiceverse’s promotional audio as being produced with 15.ai, and posted server logs as evidence. Voiceverse later acknowledged that its marketing material had been created using 15.ai and apologized, attributing the decision to its marketing team. The exchange, including 15’s profane response to the company on social media, circulated widely and was cited in later discussions of AI ethics, plagiarism, and the role of NFTs in the creative industries.

# Background

### 15.ai

**15.ai** is a free, non-commercial web application and research project that uses deep learning techniques to generate text-to-speech voices of fictional characters from popular media. It was created by an anonymous AI researcher known as 15, who began developing the system as an undergraduate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The platform became notable for producing expressive voice output from limited training data, and for enabling users to generate custom lines for characters from series such as *My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic*, *Team Fortress 2*, and *SpongeBob SquarePants*.

The developer positioned 15.ai as a non-commercial project and restricted its use through terms of service that explicitly prohibited commercial exploitation and required attribution when the system’s output was used. In late 2021, 15 publicly stated a lack of interest in integrating NFTs into the project, and expressed concerns about speculative uses of AI-generated voices.

### Voiceverse and voice NFTs

**Voiceverse** was a start-up that promoted itself as an NFT-based voice platform, offering AI-generated voices that could be purchased as NFTs and then licensed for use in online content, in-game communication, and other applications. The company marketed the idea that NFT ownership would confer commercial rights over particular synthetic voices, including the ability to deploy them in audiobooks, videos, and virtual environments.

Voiceverse’s plans included a collection described as “Origins”, a set of several thousand profile picture NFTs tied to custom voice models. Commentators noted that the business model raised questions about how the company would verify that users had legitimate rights to the voices they minted, and about the implications for professional voice actors and intellectual property owners.

### NFTs and criticism

At the time of the scandal, NFT projects were subject to extensive public scrutiny and criticism. Common concerns included the environmental impact of blockchain networks, speculative trading, and recurring allegations of fraud, plagiarism, and intellectual property infringement. Within the video game and entertainment industries, critics warned that NFT-based systems could enable predatory monetization practices and undermine existing creative professions.

The Voiceverse project was discussed in this broader context. Baker’s decision to partner with a “voice NFT” platform drew attention from both supporters of NFT experimentation and critics who viewed such projects as emblematic of perceived problems in the Web3 ecosystem.

# Discovery of plagiarism

### Promotion and partnership announcement

On 14 January 2022, Troy Baker announced on Twitter (later X) that he would be partnering with Voiceverse, using language that contrasted “hate” with “create”. The tweet linked to promotional material for Voiceverse and emphasized new tools for creators and potential ownership of AI-generated voices. The tone of the announcement and the association with NFTs drew immediate criticism from some fans, voice actors, and commentators, who cited environmental issues, speculative aspects of NFTs, and the risk that AI voices could displace human performers.

Voiceverse’s promotional video featured an AI-generated voice that the company presented as a demonstration of its own technology. Observers later identified this voice as resembling character voices available from 15.ai, with evidence suggesting that the audio had been modified in pitch.

### Identification by 15.ai

The creator of 15.ai responded on social media the same day, writing that Voiceverse’s promotional material was “lying” and that the company appeared to have used 15.ai outputs without credit. By examining server logs, 15 identified requests originating from Voiceverse that corresponded to the voice lines used in the promotional video. According to accounts of the incident, these logs showed that Voiceverse had generated lines using 15.ai’s *My Little Pony* character voices and then altered their pitch.

The use of 15.ai in this way conflicted with the service’s terms of use, which prohibited commercial use and required attribution. 15 posted screenshots of the logs and described the conduct as misrepresentation and commercial exploitation of the project’s work.

### Public exposure

The allegations spread quickly through Twitter and other platforms, amplified by users who shared the logs and commentary by 15. Coverage by technology and cryptocurrency-focused websites, as well as forums and video creators, discussed the apparent copying of 15.ai outputs and the broader issues raised by Voiceverse’s business model.

Websites such as *Web3 Is Going Just Great* and incident-tracking projects like the AI Incident Database (AIID) and the AI, Algorithmic, and Automation Incidents and Controversies (AIAAIC) later documented the case as an example of AI-related plagiarism and misuse of generative systems in an NFT context.

# Response by Voiceverse and Troy Baker

### Voiceverse’s explanation and apology

After being confronted with the evidence, Voiceverse issued a public apology acknowledging that its promotional material had been generated using 15.ai. The company stated that its marketing team had created the demo by using 15.ai without authorization or attribution, and described the decision as a result of time pressure to produce a demonstration before Voiceverse’s own technology was ready.

Voiceverse said that the relevant promotional content had been removed and pledged not to use 15.ai in that way in the future. Commentators noted that the company initially denied wrongdoing before issuing its apology, and some analyses argued that this sequence contributed to public skepticism about the explanation.

### 15.ai’s reaction

15 responded to Voiceverse’s apology on Twitter with a profane message that became widely circulated and was frequently quoted in later coverage of the incident. The response was reported to have attracted a large number of likes and retweets, and was portrayed by some observers as an expression of frustration with commercial actors who used generative AI outputs in ways that conflicted with creators’ terms and intentions.

In subsequent statements, 15 described the scandal as an example of “charlatans” misrepresenting the field of voice synthesis and emphasized objections to the commercialization of AI-generated voices through NFTs. The developer argued that such practices could harm both the public perception of AI research and the livelihoods of human voice actors.

### Troy Baker’s statements and withdrawal

Following the backlash, Baker appeared on a podcast and stated that his motivation for the partnership had been to support independent creators who could not afford professional voice actors. Critics questioned this rationale, pointing to risks that AI-generated voices might be used as lower-cost substitutes for human performers, and to the specific concerns raised by the plagiarism allegations against Voiceverse.

After criticism continued and the plagiarism reports became widely known, Baker announced that he would no longer continue the partnership with Voiceverse and apologized for his initial comments. Coverage of his decision often highlighted the combination of his initial promotional message, the subsequent revelation about Voiceverse’s use of 15.ai, and the broader debate about NFTs in creative industries.

# Ethical and legal issues

### Plagiarism and misrepresentation

Commentators and incident databases characterized Voiceverse’s conduct as plagiarism and misrepresentation. Analyses emphasized that Voiceverse had presented audio generated by 15.ai as its own proprietary technology, while using it in promotional material and in connection with NFT sales. The AIAAIC and the AI Incident Database entries on the case described it as an incident in which AI-generated audio created by a third-party non-commercial service was repurposed and sold as NFTs without acknowledgment or permission.

Writers on plagiarism and digital media ethics argued that the case illustrated how generative AI outputs can be misused in commercial settings, especially when the original systems are made available under restrictive terms that are not enforced through technical controls. Some commentary highlighted that Voiceverse’s use of 15.ai did not involve training on 15.ai models, but instead relied directly on the web interface to generate finished clips, which were then altered and marketed.

### Terms of service and enforcement

The scandal drew attention to the limitations of relying on terms of service to control the use of generative AI systems. 15.ai’s terms prohibited commercial use and required attribution, but Voiceverse was able to generate and monetize clips in violation of those conditions until the conduct was publicly exposed.

Analysts noted that log data and public communication played a central role in identifying and documenting the violation. The case was used in some discussions as an example of the need for clearer legal frameworks, technical safeguards, or licensing strategies to address unauthorized commercial use of AI-generated content.

### Impact on 15.ai and subsequent litigation

According to later retrospectives, the Voiceverse incident contributed to the eventual shutdown of public access to 15.ai, which faced concerns about copyright and legal exposure related to its use of copyrighted character voices. Commentators linked the controversy to broader tensions between innovative AI research and the intellectual property regimes of the entertainment industry.

In 2024, a group of voice actors filed a class action lawsuit in the United States against LOVO, Inc., a company associated with Voiceverse, alleging unauthorized use of their voices in AI products. Court documents cited the earlier plagiarism incident involving 15.ai as part of the case’s background, framing it as evidence of prior conduct by the company. As of mid-2025, reports indicated that the lawsuit had been allowed to proceed past initial challenges.

# Reception and commentary

### Media and incident databases

Technology and cryptocurrency-focused websites, plagiarism commentary blogs, and incident-tracking projects discussed the Voiceverse case as a significant early example of AI-related plagiarism intersecting with NFT markets. A retrospective published several years after the incident described it as a “warning” about trends that later emerged in AI commercialization and disputes over data and model usage.

The AI Incident Database cataloged the case under an incident entry describing “AI-synthetic audio sold as an NFT on Voiceverse’s platform” that had been created using 15.ai and reused without proper attribution. The AI, Algorithmic, and Automation Incidents and Controversies database similarly summarized the event as a case of plagiarized voice lines being sold as NFTs, and noted associated issues of accountability, copyright, and employment.

### Criticism from voice actors and creators

Voice actors, commentators, and content creators expressed concern that voice NFT platforms could erode opportunities for human performers by offering synthetic voices as cheaper alternatives. Some critics cited the Voiceverse scandal as evidence that such platforms might also rely on unlicensed data or outputs, compounding ethical and legal problems.

YouTubers and writers who covered the incident argued that Voiceverse’s use of 15.ai exemplified a pattern of NFT projects deploying technology in ways that disregarded the rights and preferences of creators. The scandal was referenced in broader critiques of NFTs as being associated with copying, fraud, and speculative behavior.

### Public reaction and online discourse

The exchange between 15 and Voiceverse attracted substantial attention on social media. Reports noted that 15’s response to Voiceverse’s apology received extensive engagement, with many users expressing support for the 15.ai developer and criticism of Voiceverse. Baker’s original tweet, including its framing of criticism as “hate”, was widely discussed, and his later apology and withdrawal from the partnership were also covered in gaming and entertainment news outlets.

The scandal contributed to online debates about the ethics of AI voice synthesis, the responsibilities of companies operating in the NFT space, and the relationship between independent researchers and commercial actors. Commentators connected the incident to other controversies involving NFTs and generative AI, suggesting that it foreshadowed later conflicts over training data, rights management, and attribution.

# Legacy

The Voiceverse NFT plagiarism scandal has been cited in academic, industry, and advocacy discussions as an early high-profile example of problematic interactions between generative AI systems and NFT-based business models. Retrospectives characterize the incident as illustrating several themes: the vulnerability of non-commercial AI projects to unauthorized commercial use, the challenges of enforcing terms of service, and the potential for NFT projects to amplify existing concerns about plagiarism and intellectual property.

The case influenced subsequent debates on ethical AI guidelines, documentation of AI incidents, and the design of licensing and governance mechanisms for AI-generated content. It is often mentioned alongside other controversies involving AI art and media as part of a broader discussion about how generative technologies should be used and regulated.

![Image 1](https://plagiarismtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2008/04/problogger-logo.jpg)In a “speed blogging” post from earlier this week, Darren Rowse of ProBlogger [answered a question from a reader](https://www.problogger.net/archives/2008/04/26/full-or-partial-rss-feeds/ "Problogger question") wondering if their blog should use a partial or a full RSS feed. The reader pointed out that, on the ProBlogger site, the feed was set to full but on [Digital Photography School](https://digital-photography-school.com/blog/ "Digital Photography School"), another site he operates, the feed was partial.

Rowse’s answer, however, was not a typical one to the question and, instead, offered a completely different piece of advice. According to Rowse, he prefers to keep feeds partial until the site has been around for some time and has obtained “authority in the eyes of Google”, creating what is effectively a probation period for the feed, only letting it loose when it is ready to be released.

This raises an interesting question in the full vs. partial feed debate, are the two mutually exclusive and can one site “grow” into another?

It is a topic worth debating as more and more bloggers run into this issue and try to determine what is best for their content.

#### The Basic Idea

The problem with scraping is that many sites are have their content republished heavily and never see any ill effects from it. Large, well-known blogs such as [TechCrunch](https://www.techcrunch.com/) and [Mashable](https://www.mashable.com/), are routinely republished wholesale and still maintain both their search engine ranking and their brand.

The reason is that these are well-known and trusted sites. Google and the other search engines give them priority over new sites, such as the ones spammers create, and trust that the content on them is original.

Typically, scraping most strongly affects newer and/or smaller sites. If the search engines and/or readers don’t know who you are, they could very well give the top slot to a spam blogger. However, it takes time to build up a reputation and earn a trusted position with Google.

This means that, if you start out with a full feed from day one, you are vulnerable to scrapers hijacking your position on the search engines. With their cross linking and frequent use of expired domains, it is possible a spammer could actually have more trust than a new legitimate blog, making their scraping especially damaging.

With that in mind, Rowse’s solution could actually be an answer to the problem. There are many reasons one would expect this system to work and why bloggers, especially those starting out, should at least consider it.

#### Why It Could Work

The logic behind using a feed probation period, such as what Rowse proposes, makes a lot of sense. Consider the following points:

1.  **More Original Content:** Using truncated feeds in the early stages of a site guarantees more original content on your site and that can help you build search engine trust more quickly, protecting you when you make the transition to full feeds in a drive to obtain more subscribers.
2.  **Easier Transition:** It is much easier on your readers to go from partial to full feeds rather than the other way around. If you start out with full feeds and change your mind, it could upset many readers.
3.  **Better for Servers:** New sites typically start out with very small hosts. As such, the feed can be a heavy burden until the site warrants a move to a larger “house”. A partial feed can mitigate against that.
4.  **Focus on Linkbuilding:** Most new blogs, in the early days, are focused more on linkbuilding than subscribers. As such, a truncated feed is not a major obstacle in those cases.
5.  **Promotional Event:** Many blogs turn the activation of full feeds into a promotional event and use it as a tool to lure new subscribers. If you start out with full feeds, you miss this opportunity.

But while the idea seems very sound, there are still problems with it. Putting your feed on probation might be a wonderful idea, but only if a few problems can first be overcome.

#### Issues with the System

Though a feed probation period seems to work well with what we know about search engines and scraping, it also creates more than a few problems. Those include the following:

1.  **Weakened Readership:** Many people refuse to subscribe to partial feeds and, if they see that your feed is truncated, they will not care that it is just a probation period. They will simply skip over it and likely not return.
2.  **Missed Opportunities for Pinging:** One of the great things about feeds is that you can ping the various search engines to let them know something is new. If you have a partial feed, this can lessen the impact of such pings and actually work to hurt your search engine trust, possibly negating much of the benefit you would hope to gain..
3.  **Slower Growth:** The two items above could make it more difficult to obtain inbound links since mostly subscribers link to your site, and that, when combined with the lack of pinging, could actually cause it to take longer to build search engine trust and growth in readers.

However, the biggest problem is that many, if not most, sites will never reach a point where they can safely extend their feed.

For example, after three years of operation, Plagiarism Today has well over 1000 subscribers and a PageRank of 5. A solid site in both categories, but not a huge one either. While it might seem, when combined with the site’s longevity, that it would be relatively safe from scrapers, I’ve seen many scrapings sites with a PageRank between a 3 and a 5, high enough to cause concern, and my other sites, including one run over ten years, still has an issue with copied results ranking higher than the original.

While there may come a time in which it is more safe for a site to change to a full feed, for most there is never a time where it is perfectly safe. One is still going to have to deal with scrapers, especially those that rank well in search engines, and work to protect their content from unattributed and spammy use.

As such, the feed probation period may be something of a waste since you have to take the same action regardless of whether you took advantage of it or not.

#### Conclusions

The idea of a feed probation period has some merit. However, for most blogs, it will not provide much benefit.

No matter what you do initially, when you have a full feed, scrapers are going to grab your content and, unless you are a mega-blogger, some of them are going to have the capacity to hurt you. You need to be aware of those and be ready to take action against them.

If you decide to use this method, bear in mind that, in exchange for the greataer protection during the fragile early months of the site, you will likely experience slower growth. Also realize that it will not cure your scraping ills.

Because even though Rowse never called this technique a cure for scraping and mentioned that he still deals with as many cases as he can, I know well from experience that many people are looking for a “magic bullet” to make this matter go away.

Sadly, that bullet doesn’t exist and this certainly is not it. However, it might still be a useful tool, especially for those that plan to discuss spam-friendly topics.

Just use it with caution and keep in mind that you’ll still need to take other steps to protect your work.

14.content:
When we think about AI, our first thought is often of a killer robot, rogue computer system, or humanoid child on its quest to become a real boy. Depictions of AI in film are a reflection of how people have viewed AI and similar technologies over the past century. However, the reality of what AI is differs from what we see in science fiction. AI can take many forms but it is almost never humanoid and it most certainly isn’t always bad. Our ideas of what AI is and what it can become originate from very compelling science fiction stories dating as far back as the [19th century](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/erewhon-samuel-butler) and as technology has evolved over the years, people’s ideas, hopes, and fears of AI have grown and evolved with it.

As the field of AI begins to blend the realm of reality and science fiction, let’s look at some films that offer a lens into intelligent machines, what it means to be human, and humanity’s quest to create an intelligence that may someday rival our own. Here are 15 must watch films about AI to add to your summer movie watchlist:

![Image 1](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/metropolis-robot.webp)

### 1\. Metropolis (1927)

Considered the first movie to depict artificial intelligence, this film about a dystopian future sets the stage for future AI-robot narratives. A must see for all sci-fi fans. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0017136/))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Created to sow social discord, so, bad

![Image 2](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/2001-hal-1024x538.jpg)

### 2\. 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968)

Regarded as one of the greatest and most influential films ever made, 2001: A Space Odyssey depicts AI in a new (glowing red) light, raising questions about trust and autonomy. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0062622/?ref_=nv_sr_srsg_0_tt_8_nm_0_in_0_q_2001%2520))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Not humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Programmed to be neutral but becomes bad

![Image 3](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/terminator-arnold-1024x562.jpg)

### 3\. The Terminator (1984)

This classic sci-fi thriller is the quintessential depiction of AI gone wrong. This film dives into the what-ifs of AI becoming self-aware and rejecting human authority. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0088247/?ref_=fn_all_ttl_1))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Bad (but wait for the sequel)

![Image 4](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ghost-in-the-shell-1024x576.jpg)

### 4\. Ghost in the Shell (1995)

A cyberpunk action anime thriller that explores AI consciousness, sentience, and the ethical conundrum of autonomy for artificially intelligent beings. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0113568/?ref_=nv_sr_srsg_0_tt_8_nm_0_in_0_q_Ghost%2520in%2520the%2520Shell))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Conflicted

![Image 5](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ai-movie.jpg)

### 5\. A.I. Artificial Intelligence (2001)

This sci-fi drama tells the story of a humanoid robot who embarks on the journey to become a real boy. This film raises deep ethical questions about emotional AI and the limits of empathy between AI beings and humans. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0212720/?ref_=fn_all_ttl_1))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Good

![Image 6](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/i-robot-1024x576.jpg)

### 6\. I, Robot (2004)

An action packed thriller, this film explores themes of trust, control, and morality in AI. When robots gain consciousness, do they fall in line or will they always turn against their creators? ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0343818/?ref_=fn_all_ttl_1))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Mostly bad, but misunderstood

![Image 7](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/eagle-eye-1024x589.jpg)

### 7\. Eagle Eye (2008)

In a hyperconnected world, two strangers meet in an unexpected way. This film shows how systems and surveillance powered by AI can overreach. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1059786/?ref_=fn_all_ttl_1))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Not humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Bad

![Image 8](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/wall-e-1024x576.webp)

### 8\. WALL-E (2008)

This feel-good animated classic tells the story of a lonely robot rediscovering its purpose and finding love. A look into the future of humans’ unrestrained dependence on technology. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0910970/?ref_=ls_t_1))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Semi-humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Good, and adorable

![Image 9](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/her-1024x576.jpg)

### 9\. Her (2013)

A realistic depiction of digital intimacy, this film offers a look into the emotional bond of a human and an AI system. What was once thought sci-fi is now an example of some people’s experience with AI today. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1798709/?ref_=fn_all_ttl_2))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Not humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Good

![Image 10](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ex-machina-1024x576.jpg)

### 10\. Ex Machina (2014)

This psychological thriller delves into themes of consciousness, manipulation, and power dynamics between AI and its creator. This thought provoking film will leave you wondering what it means to be human. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0470752/?ref_=nv_sr_srsg_0_tt_7_nm_1_in_0_q_ex%2520machina))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** It’s complicated

![Image 11](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/alphago-1024x663.webp)

### 11\. AlphaGo (2017)

A documentary chronicling a significant milestone in AI, a computer beating a human at the game Go. This film shows us how technology is advancing and what that may mean for the field of AI going forward.([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6700846/))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Not humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Neutral (unless you’re the human Go player who lost)

![Image 12](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/social-dilemma-1024x476.jpg)

### 12\. The Social Dilemma (2020)

This docudrama explores the real-world dangers of AI powered recommendation systems. The film shows how social media algorithms not only recommend content based on your interests but how they manipulate your behavior and exacerbate societal issues. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt11464826/?ref_=ls_t_34))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Not humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** That is the question… or as the title says, dilemma

![Image 13](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/m3gan-toys-1024x532.jpg)

### 13\. M3gan (2022)

This sci-fi horror is a warning story about using AI to replace caregiving. A creepy twist on the robot nanny, this terrifying but thoughtful film warns people of the dangers of AI assistants. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt8760708/?ref_=fn_all_ttl_2))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Bad (but her intentions are good)

![Image 14](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/the-creator-1024x538.jpg)

### 14\. The Creator (2023)

An emotional tale of a war between humans and AI where AI holds the key to peace and destruction. This film challenges assumptions about machines and humans and who is deserving of empathy. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt11858890/))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Depends on whose side you’re on

![Image 15](https://partnershiponai.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/companion-1024x576.webp)

### 15\. Companion (2025)

A thriller that examines what it means to be human, this film is a timely take on intimacy, capitalism, and the next frontier of human and AI relationships. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt26584495/?ref_=fn_all_ttl_1))

🤖 **Humanoid or not?** Humanoid  
😈 **Good or bad?** Bad, but no worse than the humans
